definition: The selective reminding test is a memory assessment that asks a person to recall learned information across repeated trials, including both unaided recall and recall helped by cues. It is used to examine episodic memory and to see whether memory problems reflect difficulty retrieving stored information rather than a failure to retain it.

reasons: The packet does not define the selective reminding test itself; it only reports use of the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test in one study, so the definition’s description of the instrument is not directly supported.

The claims that it is used to examine episodic memory and to distinguish retrieval from retention/consolidation problems go beyond what the packet supports as a general definition; those are study findings/hypotheses, not established properties of the test in the supplied text.
The wording may conflate the term with the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test, which is the only test name actually present in the packet.
The packet does not explicitly state that the test involves recall “across repeated trials.” It only names the “Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test” and reports free vs. cued recall performance.

The packet supports the retrieval-vs-consolidation distinction, but the definition’s phrasing that problems reflect difficulty “retrieving stored information rather than a failure to retain it” is not directly supported as such (the packet specifically contrasts retrieval with consolidation failure).
